title: "Just-in-Time (JIT) Compilation"
description: "Compiling program code during execution so it can be optimized for the current workload or hardware."
term: "Just-in-Time (JIT) Compilation"
letter: "J"

difficulty: "Advanced"

## Simple explanation

Just-in-time (JIT) compilation translates code into a form that can run more
efficiently while a program is running. It can reduce repeated interpretation
or optimize operations for the workload and hardware in use.

## Technical explanation

A JIT compiler typically observes or traces code at runtime, compiles selected
operations to machine code or an intermediate representation, and reuses the
compiled result. Some systems specialize compiled code based on input shapes,
types, or device configuration.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

JIT compilation can speed up numerical workloads and reduce execution overhead
when operations are repeated. Frameworks may use it to fuse operations,
optimize device execution, or generate kernels for a particular model and
input shape.

## How it works

The runtime identifies code suitable for compilation, builds an optimized
version, and executes that version on subsequent calls. Compilation has a
startup cost, and changes in shapes or execution conditions can require
additional compilations or fall back to less-specialized paths.

## Practical example

In JAX, a function can be wrapped with `jax.jit` to request compilation:

```python
import jax

compiled_function = jax.jit(my_function)
result = compiled_function(inputs)
```

The initial call may include compilation time, while repeated compatible calls
can reuse compiled code.

## Common misconceptions

- JIT does not guarantee that every function will run faster; compilation cost
  can outweigh runtime savings for small or one-off workloads.
- JIT compilation is distinct from ahead-of-time compilation, which occurs
  before program execution.
- Different input shapes or settings may trigger separate compiled versions.
